prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Startled, Somewhere, Any

outputs.L1:
Startled from its snow-day slumber by a neighbor’s mutt, it struck its buzzard’s head, then could not solve the problem of the white pine’s limbs, its wings nearly too broad for the descent it had planned. Somewhere, an awkward angel knows whether it was dead before it hit the ground. Any sinner could tell it was dead after: eyes unseen beneath bare, wrinkled lids; feet drawn up almost as high as hands.

I loved to watch thistle and millet disappear beneath it in the yard. As snow covers feathers that will still be iridescent in the spring, I remember seeing a businessman take a dripping handful of pocket change and throw it down a subway grate beside a homeless man. The coins bounced and clattered, vanishing into the humid dark. The rich man said, “Now you’re having a shitty day too.”

But it is not a shitty day, and will not be when I retrieve the bird and walk it—toes curling stiffly from a shopping bag—to a houseless scrap of oak savannah the birdseed drew it from, and dig it into deeper snow, so that what was hoarded by a man may, by the thaw, be doled.
outputs.L2:
Roused from its snow-day sleep by the neighbor’s dog, the bird struck its vulture-like head and then could not manage the puzzle of the white pine branches, its wings almost too wide for the landing it had meant to make. Somewhere, some ungainly angel may know whether it had already died before it reached the earth.

Anyone with sin in them could see it was dead afterward: its eyes hidden under bare, creased lids, its feet pulled up nearly level with its hands. I used to love watching it in the yard as thistle and millet vanished beneath its body.

While snow falls over feathers that will still shine with iridescence when spring comes, I think of once seeing a businessman scoop up a wet handful of coins from his pocket and fling them through a subway grate beside a homeless man. The change rang and skipped as it disappeared into the damp darkness. The wealthy man said, “Now you’re having a shitty day too.”

But this is not a shitty day, and it still will not be when I pick up the bird and carry it—its stiff toes curling from a shopping bag—to the homeless remnant of oak savannah from which the birdseed had lured it, then bury it in deeper snow, so that what one man kept for himself may be distributed when the thaw arrives.
outputs.L3:
A bird, startled by the sudden barking and movement of a neighbor’s dog, panicked and tried to escape through the branches of the snow-covered white pine. In its confusion, it misjudged the whitened tangle of needles and limbs and crashed fatally among them. What had been a quick, bright life in the yard ended abruptly in the cold.

The speaker remembers the bird with affection, recalling the simple pleasure of watching it feed on thistle and millet scattered outside. It had been a familiar presence, small and lively, part of the daily winter scene. Its visits had offered a quiet kind of companionship, a reminder of life persisting through snow and cold.

Now the bird’s body lies in the snow, still and exposed. The description of its death is both tender and unflinching: the speaker sees not only the delicate beauty of the creature but also the blunt physical fact of its broken body. The snow that once formed part of the bird’s winter world has become its resting place, emphasizing both the softness and the severity of the moment.

This sight leads the speaker to remember another act of cruelty: a businessman throwing coins down a subway grate beside a homeless man. The gesture was not generous but mocking, placing help just out of reach and turning another person’s need into an opportunity for humiliation. The memory deepens the speaker’s awareness of suffering, waste, and the casual harm living beings inflict on one another.

In response to the bird’s death, the speaker decides to bury it in deeper snow. This burial is both an act of care and a gesture of return. The seeds the bird had stored or eaten—thistle, millet, and other small remnants of its life—may, when the thaw comes, pass back into the earth. In that way, the bird’s brief life and sudden death may become part of the land again, transformed into renewal when winter loosens its hold.
outputs.L4:
In the middle of winter, when the snow had settled over the savannah in a single pale sheet and the grasses stood through it like the ribs of something sleeping, I found the bird.

It lay at the edge of the path, just beyond the packed trail where boots and skis had hardened the snow into a gray crust. At first I mistook it for a curled leaf, one of the few the wind had not carried off, or perhaps a scrap of bark shaken loose from the oaks. But then I saw the small perfection of its body: the folded wing, the narrow feet drawn close, the head turned slightly to one side as if listening. Its feathers were not bright in the winter light. They held the muted colors of the season—brown, ash, a little rust, a little cream—so that even in death it seemed to belong exactly where it was.

There was no sign of violence. No blood marked the snow. No scattered feathers told of a hawk’s descent. It may have struck a window, or grown too cold, or simply reached the end of whatever measure had been given to it. The body was light when I lifted it, almost weightless, and yet it carried the heaviness of being a body no longer inhabited. I could feel through my glove the fragile architecture of its bones. It was astonishing that such a thing had ever flown.

Holding it, I remembered the sound of birds in warmer months, how they filled the savannah before sunrise, hidden in grasses and branches, making the air seem woven with calls. I remembered their sudden movements from stem to stem, their insistence, their hunger, their small territorial songs. In summer they are so quick that they appear less like animals than like thoughts crossing the open field. In winter, one dead bird in the hand becomes entirely physical. It becomes feather, bone, beak, claw. It becomes evidence.

I could have left it there. That would have been natural enough. The cold would have preserved it for a while; a fox or crow might have found it; the thaw would eventually have taken it down into the soil. Nothing in the world required my intervention. And yet something in me resisted the idea of leaving the bird on the trodden edge of the path, where it might be stepped on, kicked aside, or slowly flattened into the dirty snow by the passing of indifferent feet.

So I carried it away from the trail, out toward a place where the grasses were taller and the snow had not been broken. Each step made a soft, compact sound. The oaks stood black and patient around me, their branches bare except for a few stubborn leaves trembling in the wind. The sky had the low metallic color of late afternoon. It was not a solemn landscape exactly, but it was quiet enough to receive solemnity.

As I walked, I thought of another winter scene, one I had heard about and could not forget. A homeless man had been sleeping near the back of a building, wrapped in blankets against the cold. Some people—young, perhaps drunk, perhaps only bored in the terrible way people become when they have never been taught to see another life as real—had found him there. They did not offer food or help or even leave him in peace. They tormented him. They poured something on him, or threw things, or shouted and laughed; the details shift in memory, but the cruelty remains constant. What stayed with me was not only that they harmed him, but that they treated his vulnerability as an invitation.

There are many ways to fail the living. Most of them do not look dramatic. We step around people. We look away. We tell ourselves we have nothing to give, or that giving would not solve anything, or that someone else must be responsible. We store up warmth, money, time, attention. We become practiced in the art of keeping what we have. Hoarding is not only the accumulation of objects; it is also the refusal to let care move outward.

The bird in my hand was not the man. A burial for a bird would not undo cruelty done to a human being. It would not feed anyone, house anyone, or make the world just. I knew that. Still, the mind makes associations according to its own moral weather. The small dead body, the winter field, the memory of a person left exposed to the malice of others—all of it gathered together. I felt, obscurely, that how we touch the dead has something to do with how we regard the living. To handle even a bird with tenderness is to practice a form of attention opposed to contempt.

I found a shallow hollow beneath a clump of grass where the snow had drifted loosely. With my mitten I cleared a small space down to the matted stems. The earth beneath was frozen and could not be opened, so I made the only grave winter allowed: a bed of grass and snow. I placed the bird there carefully, as though it might be uncomfortable otherwise, as though the angle of the wing still mattered. Then I covered it, first with the loose straw-colored grasses, then with snow. The whiteness received it completely.

It was not much. No prayer came to me, at least not in words. But the gesture itself felt like a sentence spoken in a language older than speech: you were here; you are not nothing; you may return.

Returning the bird to the savannah did not feel like possession, but the opposite. I had taken it up only in order to give it back. The field had fed it once, sheltered it, hidden it, lifted it into air. Now the field would keep it. In time, when the snow melted and the ground softened, what remained would enter the roots of grass, the bodies of insects, the hunger of other birds. Nothing would be wasted. The world, when left to its deeper laws, is not a hoarder. It redistributes endlessly.

Perhaps that is why the act mattered to me. Against the meanness that clutches and guards, against the indifference that passes by, against the cruelty that sees weakness and moves toward it with violence, there was this small contrary motion: to notice, to lift, to carry, to return. A dead bird in winter cannot be rescued. But it can be honored. And sometimes dignity is not a grand declaration, but a quiet rearrangement of what has been abandoned.

When I stepped back, the place of burial was almost invisible. Snow blew lightly over my tracks. The grasses moved in the wind, and the oaks stood as they had stood before. Nothing had changed in any obvious way. Yet I felt that something had been answered, if only briefly and locally, in the only terms available: cold with covering, death with attention, abandonment with care.
outputs.L5:
**Startled Somewhere**

Somewhere in the quiet hours of the night, a small sound echoed through the empty street. It was not loud, but it was enough to make Mara stop walking. Startled, she turned her head and listened carefully, her heart beating faster than before.

There was no one behind her, and the wind moved gently through the trees. Still, she felt as if something had changed. Any ordinary person might have ignored the noise and continued home, but Mara was curious. She stepped closer to the alley beside the old bookstore and saw a tiny kitten hiding behind a box.

With a soft smile, Mara knelt down and reached out her hand. The kitten stared at her for a moment, then slowly came forward. Somewhere between fear and trust, the little creature decided she was safe.

Mara picked it up carefully and held it close. What had startled her at first became the beginning of an unexpected friendship.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about finding a dead bird in the snow after it crashes into a pine tree, weaving in a memory of cruelty on a subway and ending with a gesture of restitution to nature.
counterfactuals.output:
The bird lay beneath the pine as if the tree had dreamed it and then let it fall. A small brown sentence in the snow, unfinished. Above it, the branches held their green severity, needled and silent, dusted white where the storm had touched them gently. I could see the place where it must have struck: a quiver of loosened powder on one bough, a dark bead of sap shining like an eye.

I knelt. The snow accepted my knees without complaint. The bird’s wings were folded close, not broken-looking, only private, as though it had tucked itself into sleep mid-flight and forgotten the world was hard. Around its beak, crystals gathered; on its breast, the faintest yellow, like a candle seen through paper.

I thought of the subway years ago, winter then too, everyone sealed in wool and impatience. A man dropped his bag of oranges and they rolled under the seats, bright little planets escaping. No one helped. Someone laughed. Someone kicked one farther down the car, and I—young, afraid of appearing tender—watched the fruit bruise against the filthy floor. The man bent alone, his ears red, gathering what he could while the train lurched and the rest of us practiced our cruelty by calling it nothing.

How many times does the heart strike the invisible glass of itself? How often do we mistake silence for innocence?

I lifted the bird with my scarf. It weighed almost nothing, which made it harder to bear. At the base of the pine, where the roots made a dark cradle in the snow, I dug with my hands until I reached the leaf-mold beneath, the old brown warmth of the earth remembering itself. I laid the bird there, covered it with soil and needles, then broke the last apple from my pocket into pieces and scattered them for whatever hunger came next.

Above me, the pine released a soft fall of snow, as if absolving no one, but blessing the attempt.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, lyrical flash piece in one paragraph about a buzzard or large bird killed in winter, with themes of hoarding, poverty, birdseed, and the thaw redistributing what humans keep.
counterfactuals.output: All winter the buzzard lay at the edge of the county road, black wings folded like a poor man’s coat, head tucked into the sleet as if ashamed of its own hunger, while in the houses above the ditch we measured flour by the cup, beans by the fist, kerosene by the blue breath it gave the lamp, and locked away sacks of birdseed from the mice, from the neighbors, from whatever in us wanted to scatter and be done. The feeder hung empty most mornings because we were saving what was meant for saving, because the cardinals could wait, because poverty teaches even kindness to clench its teeth; yet the dead bird kept receiving—snow, cinders, the dull coin of a hubcap’s shine, the prayers of crows who came not to mourn but inventory. Then thaw arrived with its wet mouth and loosened everything: roof-ice, cellar doors, the hard crust over the garden, the banked-up secrets of barns; it ran brown through the yards and lifted the birdseed we had spilled or hidden, millet and cracked corn sluicing from split bags, from porch corners, from the cuffs of our thrift, down to the roadside where the buzzard opened, not by will but weather, and gave back what it had been keeping—feather, bone, a last dark ration—to the ditchwater’s slow republic. By evening the finches descended on the mud like sparks, pecking among thawed rot and seed alike, and we watched from our windows with our hands in our pockets, feeling the cupboards behind us, feeling how little we owned that water could not find, soften, shoulder loose, and carry toward another hunger.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary prose poem in the style of bleak Midwestern nature writing: a neighbor’s dog wakes the speaker, a bird dies in the yard, and the speaker recalls a businessman throwing coins down a subway grate beside a homeless man.
counterfactuals.output:
Before dawn, the neighbor’s dog begins its argument with the dark.

Not barking, exactly. More like a machine trying to turn over in the cold, each sound dragged up from the gravel of its chest. I lie there and listen to it worry the same invisible thing beyond the fence: raccoon, wind, the moon caught in the bare maple like a hubcap. The house clicks around me. The furnace exhales its warm, dusty breath. Out past the window the fields are still black, stitched with the white seams of old snow.

By morning the dog is quiet, and there is a bird in the yard.

A small brown one, common as a thumbprint. It lies on its side beneath the kitchen window, one wing opened as if making a point it has forgotten. The grass around it is stiff with frost. Nothing in the yard seems surprised. The lilacs hold their dead blossoms. The garden hose, curled beside the spigot, keeps its green counsel. Even the sky has taken on that flat Midwestern look, the color of dishwater in a rented room.

I stand there with my coffee going cold and think of a man in a wool coat, years ago, in a city underground.

He was some kind of businessman, or had arranged himself to look like one: polished shoes, briefcase, the severe little shine of success. Beside him sat a homeless man with his back against the tile, hands cupped in his lap, not asking so much as enduring the shape of asking. Trains breathed in the tunnels. People stepped around him with the careful blindness of the employed.

The businessman reached into his pocket and brought out coins.

For one second I believed in the old forms: mercy, accident, the small repair. But he did not drop them into the man’s hands. He smiled—almost privately—and tossed them through the grate at his feet. One by one they rang on the iron, flashed, vanished into the dark below the platform. Quarters, maybe. Dimes. Little moons falling where no hand could follow.

The homeless man looked at the grate. Then at the businessman. Then at nothing.

This is what returns to me while I carry the bird on a shovel toward the back fence, its body light as a question nobody meant to ask. The dog watches from next door, muzzle silvered, eyes yellow with having seen too much of morning. A truck moves along the county road, dragging its long sound behind it. Somewhere under the soil, roots keep their blind accounts.

I tip the shovel.

The bird enters the weeds without ceremony. There is no lesson in it, unless the lesson is that the world is mostly made of things falling: coins into darkness, birds from the air, the heart from its small height again and again. The dog sniffs once at the fence and turns away. The day opens, gray and practical, over the harvested fields.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an unsettling, compassionate vignette about discovering a dead iridescent bird under snow, including religious imagery like sinners and angels, and closing with the speaker burying it near an oak savannah.
counterfactuals.output:
At first I thought it was a shard of bottle glass, blue-green and wickedly bright beneath the crust of snow. The morning had been so still that every twig wore its white sleeve, and my own breath seemed like an interruption. I bent down with the small guilt of a trespasser and brushed the snow away.

It was a bird.

Death had not made it humble. Its throat shone violet, then emerald, then black, depending on how my shadow crossed it. Each feather held a little weather, a little oil-slick heaven. One wing was folded neatly against its side; the other had opened just enough to suggest surprise, or surrender. Its feet, fine as burnt matchsticks, were clenched around nothing.

I stood there longer than I meant to. There was something indecent about such color in the frozen ditch, something almost liturgical. The world around it was all ash and linen, and there it lay like a dropped ornament from an angel’s sleeve. I thought of sinners in old paintings, faces turned upward, mouths open to receive either mercy or flame. I thought of angels too—not the gentle ones from cards, but the terrible ones, ringed with eyes, carrying announcements no body could survive.

The bird looked as if it had fallen from one kingdom into another and found both inhospitable.

I took off my gloves and lifted it in my bare hands. It was lighter than an apology. The cold had made it rigid, but not ugly. Nothing had fed on it yet. No fox had nosed it open, no crow had translated it back into hunger. For a moment I felt entrusted with a secret too small for doctrine and too large for speech.

“I’m sorry,” I said, though I did not know for what: the storm, the glass sky, the hard white ground, my warm animal life continuing above it.

Behind the road, the land opened into the tawny remnant of an oak savannah, bur oaks standing with their dark, muscled arms spread wide over the snow. I carried the bird there, cupped between my palms like a coal that would not warm me. At the edge of the grasses, where the snow thinned and the earth gave a little under my heel, I dug with a flat stone until the soil accepted my fingers.

Then I laid the iridescent body down, covered it gently, and left it buried near the oaks—under the sleeping grass, beneath the patient trees, where sinners and angels might pass without knowing what brightness had been hidden there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary paragraph with no line breaks about a winter bird collision, birdseed, homelessness, and economic cruelty, using vivid sensory details and ending on the idea that spring thaw will redistribute what was hoarded.
counterfactuals.output: The sparrow struck the plate glass with a sound like a knuckle on a coffin lid, a small brown burst against the pane where the warm storelight shone over sacks of millet and sunflower hearts stacked higher than a hungry man’s shoulders, their plastic seams sweating faintly with the smell of dust, oil, and dry fields. Outside, winter had lacquered the sidewalk in gray ice, and under the bank awning a man slept inside two coats and a cardboard sign gone soft with sleet, while above him the feeder display glittered with red ribbons and promises of generosity for creatures light enough to be pitied. The bird lay stunned in the gutter, its claws opening and closing on nothing, its breast ticking beneath a crust of snow, and passing boots ground salt into the curb as if the whole city had been taught to preserve only what could be purchased. Inside, the cashier counted coins, the landlord counted doors, the manager counted losses, and the rich counted themselves innocent behind glass so clean it reflected the poor as weather. But beneath the frozen street, black water was already nosing through the pipes and roots, patient as a verdict, and when the spring thaw comes it will loosen every locked granary, lift the swollen river over its banks, and redistribute what was hoarded.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
